ModelCharacter: A long, moderate-beam Gulfstar trawler using essentially the Gulfstar 43 Motorsailer hull without the sailing rig. DesignLineage: The Gulfstar 43 Trawler was produced from 1972–1977 on the Gulfstar 43 Motorsailer hull.
The original version used a traditional trunk-cabin arrangement.
A 1975 Mk II redesign added a full-width aft deck, revised flybridge and larger master stateroom, along with a full teak interior.
The 43 remains a valid powerboat despite its sail-derived hull; the motorsailer is a separate configuration outside this B-Atlas record.
OwnershipCharacter: A comfortable and efficient offshore-oriented cruiser at displacement-like speeds, with protected running gear and useful engine-room access. Twin machinery, extensive teak, aging tanks and large vintage systems make ownership materially more demanding than the 36.

ModelVariations.Name: Layout and engine variation
ModelVariations.Description: Island Gypsy models were offered in Sedan, Europa, Fisherman, Classic and motor-cruiser configurations with materially different layouts and engine packages.

ModelCharacter: The working-boat member of the Island Gypsy 32 family: a large-cockpit fisherman with basic overnight accommodation, smaller flybridge and materially higher available speed than the sedan trawlers. It looks and behaves more like a compact utility cruiser than a traditional slow trawler.
DesignLineage: Built from the same two-piece semi-displacement hull mold used for the Island Gypsy 32 Sedan.
The Fisherman layout was influenced by traditional Australian fishing-boat design.
Its enlarged cockpit, simpler accommodation and optional higher-output single or twin diesels distinguish it from the Sedan and Europa.
It is therefore a true configuration/model variant, not a duplicate 32 Sedan identity.
OwnershipCharacter: Less residential and more utilitarian than the other 32s, with good cockpit access and relatively simple accommodation. Higher-output engine installations can make propulsion cost and access more significant than on the slow single-Lehman sedan versions.

ModelVariations.Name: 1988 keel revision
ModelVariations.Description: Keel design was revised in 1988 to reduce vibration.

ModelCharacter: A full-keel semi-displacement fishing/weekend cruiser with distinctive Downeast styling, enormous 110-square-foot cockpit and surprisingly complete four-berth cabin. It combines a single gasoline inboard with 14–15-knot cruise and unusually secure working decks.
DesignLineage: Produced from 1987–1990.
The Alura 30 was one of Luhrs' more cruising-oriented models rather than a conventional convertible sportfisher.
The keel was redesigned in 1988 specifically to reduce vibration problems.
The larger Alura 35 shared the same broad multipurpose fishing/cruising concept but was a separate hull.
OwnershipCharacter: One inboard and full keel are mechanically straightforward, although gasoline fuel burn is substantial relative to a diesel trawler. The 1988 keel revision makes year important; steering linkage, shaft alignment, fuel tanks and cockpit structure should be checked.

ModelVariations.Description: The 32 design evolved during its long production run; later examples and published specifications can include platforms or appendages that bring overall length close to the later 34 while the core model identity remains 32.

ModelCharacter: The model that turned Nordic Tug from a charming niche 26-footer into a serious cruising brand. The 32 combines a raised pilothouse, full-keel prop protection and single-diesel economy with enough salon and cabin space for extended cruising by a couple.
DesignLineage: Introduced in 1985 after the success of the Nordic Tug 26.
Designed by Lynn Senour around the same classic tug profile and efficient semi-displacement philosophy.
Early boats used lower-horsepower diesels; later production gained substantially more power while retaining economical displacement-speed operation.
The 32 later evolved into the Nordic Tug 34 as the transom/swim platform was integrated and the interior was refreshed.
OwnershipCharacter: One of the more approachable traditional cruising boats for a couple: straightforward single-diesel machinery, protected running gear and strong owner support. Interior space is efficient rather than expansive, and older examples vary considerably by engine and refit history.

ModelCharacter: A Canadian-market Taiwan-built sedan trawler from 1980, combining broad covered walkaround decks, an unusually teak-rich interior and a single Ford Lehman diesel in a roomy 36-foot cruising package. It is a separate Oceania Yachts identity, not an Ocean Alexander model.
DesignLineage: Canadian Yachting tested the first Oceania 36 Sedan imported to Canada in 1980 by Donaldson Yacht Sales of Port Credit, Ontario.
The boat was marketed under the Oceania Yachts name as part of a range of Oriental trawlers; available companion configurations included aft-cabin styles.
Its U.S.-origin design and Taiwan construction reflect the broad late-1970s/early-1980s trawler-import market rather than Ocean Alexander's documented model lineage.

B-Atlas corrected the prior Ocean Alexander attribution because exact-model research found no credible historical Ocean Alexander 36 Sedan, while contemporary documentation clearly establishes the Oceania 36 Sedan.
OwnershipCharacter: Single-engine simplicity and excellent sheltered deck circulation make the boat attractive for slow cruising. Extensive teak, vintage deckhouse construction, old tanks/windows and the rarity of the Oceania marque make condition and prior restoration more important than model-specific parts availability.

ModelVariations.Name: Prairie 36 / Atlantic 37 lineage
ModelVariations.Description: After Prairie closed, Atlantic Yachts acquired the Prairie 36 molds and reintroduced the design as the Atlantic 37 Double Cabin.

ModelCharacter: A compact American-built Jack Hargrave trawler created specifically to fill the late-1970s gap for an economical, genuinely livable cruiser under 30 feet. Its semi-displacement hull, full keel, very wide 12-foot beam and single Perkins diesel deliver exceptional interior volume and 6–7-knot fuel economy.
DesignLineage: Prairie Boat Works commissioned J.B. Hargrave in 1977 to design a semi-displacement trawler under 30 feet; production began in 1978.
The 29 Coastal Cruiser became Prairie's defining powerboat and used a rounded-bottom/soft-chine semi-displacement hull with full keel.
The success of the 29 directly led Prairie to commission the larger 36 Coastal Cruiser using the same broad design philosophy.
When Prairie closed in early 1982, Atlantic Yachts acquired the molds and tooling and reintroduced the 29 lineage as the Atlantic 30.
OwnershipCharacter: Very simple mechanically and exceptionally economical, usually with one small diesel and protected shaft. The unusually broad beam provides excellent interior room but prevents normal road trailering; after nearly five decades, tanks, decks, windows, wiring and repower quality matter far more than original engine specification.

ModelVariations.Name: RF-246 layout and propulsion families
ModelVariations.Description: Historical Sedan Cruiser, Custom Wheelhouse and later Digby/Halifax/Yarmouth arrangements share the RF-246 platform but differ materially in interior layout, power and tankage.

ModelCharacter: The classic Canadian 'trailerable trawler' version of the RF-246: a sedan cabin extended aft for a larger dinette and galley, with a covered cockpit and economical diesel propulsion. It is one of the earliest boats to prove that a cruising couple could combine real coastal capability with road portability.
DesignLineage: The RF-246 Sedan Cruiser grew from the same Bob Rosborough hull first delivered in 1987.
Period reviews describe the Sedan as the longer-cabin cruising alternative to the Custom Wheelhouse, with substantially more enclosed living space.
Diesel inboard, diesel sterndrive and outboard power were all used across the broad RF-246 family; this B-Atlas record represents the legacy diesel Sedan Cruiser identity.
After Eastern Boats acquired the molds, the cruising-sedan tradition continued in modern 246 layouts such as the Yarmouth rather than under the old Sedan Cruiser Diesel name.
OwnershipCharacter: A rare combination of simple diesel economy, trailerability and genuine overnight accommodation. Older Volvo/Yanmar propulsion, fuel tanks, cabin systems and trailers deserve age-specific inspection, but the hull itself has a strong reputation for durability and rough-water security.
